## The Fed held on October 28. Both dissenters wanted a hike.

A 10-2 vote kept the federal funds target at 3.75 to 4 percent. The dissenters wanted an increase; the companion note explains the operating settings.

1 November 2026

[Archive portrait of Kevin Warsh in a navy suit at his May 22, 2026 swearing-in ceremony.](file:///A:/Capital%20Chronicle/Worktrees/ContentOps/codex-publisher-backlog/docs/publisher/CC-074-private-20261101/media/archive-warsh-20260522.jpg)

Commons crop; no further edits.](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Federal_Reserve_Chair_Kevin_Warsh_delivers_remarks_at_his_swearing-in_ceremony_in_the_East_Room_of_the_White_House,_Friday,_May_22,_2026._(Cropped).jpg) · [Reuse terms](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Template:PD-USGov)*

*Retrospective analysis, written on 1 November 2026 (GMT+7).*

An unchanged rate can still contain a pointed disagreement. On October 28, 2026, the Federal Reserve's policy committee voted 10-2 to keep the federal funds target range at 3.75 to 4 percent, according to its [October 28 statement](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm). Both dissenters wanted a quarter-percentage-point increase.

Capital Chronicle's reading is that the decision and its implementation answer different questions. The vote establishes the target range and the direction of disagreement. The companion note sets out the rates and instructions used to implement that stance. A reader needs both documents to distinguish the policy choice from its operating settings.

#### A hold with dissent in one direction

Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voted against the action because they preferred to raise the target range by a quarter percentage point at that meeting. That makes the direction of dissent clear: they favored an increase, while the approved action maintained the range.

The statement described economic activity as expanding strongly, domestic spending as resilient and inflation as elevated. It also said accumulating more information would help the Committee determine the stance appropriate for a timely return to its 2 percent inflation goal. That is the Committee's published assessment; it should not be turned into a separate explanation attributed to either dissenter.

The strongest countercase to a looming-hike interpretation is the decision itself: ten members approved keeping the range unchanged. The two dissenters' preference is evidence of disagreement at this meeting, not a forecast of the next vote. Reading the split as a timetable for higher rates would give it a meaning the vote alone cannot establish.

[What did the majority approve, and in which direction did the dissenters disagree?](file:///A:/Capital%20Chronicle/Worktrees/ContentOps/codex-publisher-backlog/docs/publisher/CC-074-private-20261101/media_assets/cc074-fomc-20261028-vote-direction.png)
*A two-category vote comparison joins the strength of the majority to the direction of dissent. It prevents an undifferentiated split-vote graphic from suggesting the dissenters wanted a cut or that the committee was evenly divided. Name the two dissenters beside their preference; do not invent a majority-member roster. · Source: [Federal Reserve Board](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a.htm)*

#### One target range, several operating rates

The [companion implementation note](https://www.federalreserve.gov/newsevents/pressreleases/monetary20261028a1.htm) describes decisions to carry out the October 28 policy stance. The Board of Governors unanimously maintained interest paid on reserve balances at 3.90 percent, effective October 29. The directive to the New York Fed's trading desk, also effective October 29, instructed it to undertake operations as necessary to maintain the federal funds rate within the 3.75 to 4 percent target range.

The same directive set standing overnight repo operations at 4.0 percent and the standing overnight reverse repo offering rate at 3.75 percent. In a related action, the Board unanimously approved the primary credit rate at its existing 4.0 percent level. The note therefore assigns some identical numbers to different instruments; it does not combine those instruments into a single rate.

The 3.90 percent reserve-balances setting is not a substitute label for the 3.75 to 4 percent federal funds target range. One is an individual rate; the other is the interval the desk is instructed to maintain. Likewise, unanimous Board actions on reserve interest and primary credit should not be mistaken for unanimity in the 10-2 FOMC decision.
